name: Deep Orange-Coloured Brown
lede: Deep Orange-Coloured Brown is one of the descriptive color names used in the early nineteenth century to catalogue minerals, plants and animals, and it matches the red-brown of hematite and the cattail's spike.

sections.title: A name from a naturalist's chart
sections.body:
This name belongs to Patrick Syme's color chart for natural history, which Baty traces in her book on nature's palette [1]. Syme took five new terms from Sowerby's *A New Elucidation of Colours* of 1809, and this name is one of the five, together with two oranges and two purples [1]. Our library dates its earliest record to 1821, from the Werner nomenclature, while Baty places Syme's terminology earlier in the century, so the exact year is uncertain [1][3].

The name is plain on purpose. It reads like a recipe: take a deep brown, lean it toward orange. A naturalist could use it to compare a mineral, a feather and a leaf by one shared scale.

sections.title: What it was matched to
sections.body:
Baty's plates show the chart in use. The plates pair it with the spike of a cattail reed, drawn in Palmstruch's *Svensk Botanik* of 1807, and on specimens of hematite from Sowerby's *British Mineralogy* [1]. The same chart section groups it with the reds and browns, next to Deep Reddish Brown [1].

See [[deep-reddish-brown]], [[reddish-brown]], [[brownish-orange]] and [[chestnut]] for the nearby names, and [[reddish-orange]] for the chart's own neighbor above it [1][3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings this color appears in 1,137, or 4.78%, as photographed, and it is more common than 87% of the named colors [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 71% of the 764 paintings measured by lightness rank [3]. It peaks in the 1200s, at 10.6% of the 142 paintings from that period, 2.4 times the expected rate [3].

It is most over-represented in Tibet, at 7.4 times expected, 17 of 47 paintings [3]. John Singer Sargent uses it most often, in 10 of 287 works here, though no painter stands out against the museum baseline [3]. It shares canvases with Ferruginous and Mahogany Brown more than chance (lift 5.1 and 2.9) [3].

The earliest match is dated 1000, 821 years before the name's earliest record, so it is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of the dye or pigment [3].
